title: Mozilla's AI-Powered Firefox Security Hardening: 423 Bugs Fixed in April
description: Mozilla used access to Claude Mythos preview to locate and fix hundreds of vulnerabilities in Firefox. The transformation was dramatic: from fixing 20-30 security bugs per month through 2025 to 423 in April 2026 alone. Key factors: (1) models became much more capable, (2) dramatic improvements in techniques for harnessing models - steering them, scaling them, and stacking them to generate signal and filter noise. The report details specific bugs found, including a 20-year old XSLT bug and a 15-year-old bug in the <legend> element. Many attempts were blocked by Firefox's existing defense-in-depth measures. This represents a major shift in AI-assisted security research, moving from unwanted 'slop' bug reports to high-quality, actionable security insights.
author: Simon Willison (citing Mozilla)

title: Shopify's River: Public-First AI Agent Development & Lehrwerkstatt Culture
description: Simon Willison highlights Tobias Lütke's description of Shopify's internal AI coding agent 'River'. Key innovation: River operates entirely in public on Shopify's Slack, refusing direct messages and insisting on public channels. This creates a 'Lehrwerkstatt' (teaching workshop) environment where all conversations are searchable and anyone can jump in to learn. In Tobias's channel alone, over 100 people actively participate - reacting to threads, adding context, helping with reviews, and learning through observation. The concept of 'osmosis learning' - learning by being near the work without requiring curriculum or training plans, just maximum visibility. Similar to how Midjourney's early success was tied to public Discord channels forcing users to share prompts and learn from each other. This represents a significant organizational shift toward transparent, observable AI-assisted development.
author: Simon Willison / Tobias Lütke

title: Using Claude Code: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of HTML
description: Thariq Shihipar (Claude Code team at Anthropic) advocates for HTML over Markdown as an output format to request from Claude. Since GPT-4 days, Markdown was preferred due to 8,192 token limit making token-efficiency worthwhile. But HTML enables richer outputs: SVG diagrams, interactive widgets, in-page navigation, making information more pleasant to navigate. Simon Willison tested this by having GPT-5.5 create an HTML explanation of the copy.fail Linux security exploit. The result: a rich, interactive technical document with color-coded callouts, tables comparing patterns to purposes, and detailed step-by-step explanations. This suggests a shift from Markdown-first to HTML-first for AI-generated explanations, especially for complex technical content.
author: Simon Willison / Thariq Shihipar

title: LLM 0.32a2: OpenAI's /v1/responses Endpoint for Reasoning Models
description: Simon Willison's LLM tool release introduces support for OpenAI's new `/v1/responses` endpoint (instead of `/v1/chat/completions`) for reasoning-capable models. This enables interleaved reasoning across tool calls for GPT-5 class models. Users can now see summarized reasoning tokens displayed in a different color to standard error, with flags `-R` or `--hide-reasoning` to control visibility. This represents OpenAI's continued evolution toward more transparent reasoning models, giving developers insight into the model's thinking process while maintaining clean output for end-users.
author: Simon Willison

title: GitLab Act 2: Agentic Era Workforce Restructuring
description: GitLab's announcement on 'workforce reduction' and 'structural and strategic decisions' for the agentic era reveals major shifts: (1) Reducing number of countries with small teams by up to 30%, (2) Flattening organization - removing up to three layers of management so leaders are closer to work, (3) Reorganizing R&D into ~60 smaller, more empowered teams with end-to-end ownership (nearly doubling independent teams), (4) Retiring CREDIT values framework (Collaboration, Results, Efficiency, Diversity, Inclusion, Transparency) for new values: Speed with Quality, Ownership Mindset, Customer Outcomes. Most insight: 'The agentic era multiplies demand for software' - as cost of producing software collapses, demand will expand. Jevons paradox applied to AI: efficiency increases consumption, not decreases it.
author: Simon Willison (analyzing GitLab)

title: James Shore: AI Coding Agents Must Reduce Maintenance Costs
description: Critical insight from James Shore: 'Your AI coding agent needs to reduce your maintenance costs. Not by a little bit, either.' If you write code twice as quick, you better hope you've halved your maintenance costs. Three times as productive? One third the maintenance costs. Otherwise, you're screwed - trading temporary speed boost for permanent indenture. The math: if you double output and double maintenance costs, you've quadrupled maintenance burden (2x2). If you double output and hold maintenance steady, you've still doubled maintenance (2x1). The only way AI coding tools create sustainable value is if they decrease maintenance costs by exactly the inverse of the rate they add code. This challenges the current AI coding narrative that focuses on generation speed over long-term maintainability.
author: James Shore (cited by Simon Willison)

title: Zombie Internet: AI Writing is Breaking Our Brains
description: Jason Koebler's excellent, angry piece on how AI writing online is becoming impossible to avoid. Introduces 'Zombie Internet' concept: not just bots talking to bots (Dead Internet), but 'people talking to bots, people talking to people, people creating AI agents and then instructing them to interact with people.' It's people using AI talking to people not using AI, and people using AI talking to other people using AI. It's influencer hustlebros teaching each other how to make AI influencers, automated YouTube channels and blogs spamming the internet for money. It's AI summaries of real books sold as the book itself. Filtering AI content is mentally exhausting and starting to distort regular human writing styles. This piece captures the growing fatigue and cognitive cost of living in an AI-saturated internet.
author: Jason Koebler (cited by Simon Willison)

title: Using LLM in Shebang Lines:Executable English Scripts
description: Simon Willison explores using LLM directly in script shebang lines, inspired by Kim_Bruning on Hacker noting 'you can put a shebang on an english text file now.' Examples: (1) Simple: `#!/usr/bin/env -S llm -f` with prompt text, (2) With tools: `#!/usr/bin/env -S llm -T llm_time -f` to enable time calculations, (3) Complex YAML templates defining extra tools as Python functions, then executing with arguments like `./calc.sh 'what is 2344 * 5252 + 134' --td`. The `--td` flag shows tool debug output. This pattern turns natural language into executable scripts, with LLM handling the heavy lifting. Simon even built a version using Datasette SQL API to answer questions about blog content. This represents a fascinating fusion of traditional Unix scripting philosophy with LLM capabilities.
author: Simon Willison

title: Notes on the xAI/Anthropic Data Center Deal
description: Simon Willison analyzes Anthropic's deal with SpaceX/xAI to use 'all of the capacity of their Colossus data center.' The announcement came at Code w/ Claude 2026 event. Willison examines the implications of this partnership between two leading AI companies, considering data center capacity, compute constraints, and the strategic value of infrastructure partnerships in the AI race. This deal highlights the growing importance of compute infrastructure as a competitive moat in AI development.
author: Simon Willison

title: OpenAI's WebRTC Problem: Audio Quality Trade-offs in Voice AI
description: Luke Curley identifies a critical issue with OpenAI's low-latency voice AI: WebRTC is designed to degrade and drop audio during poor network conditions to keep latency low. For conference calls, this makes sense - rapid back-and-forth is essential. But for voice AI prompts, this is problematic: users would rather wait 200ms for accurate prompts than get distorted audio from dropped packets. As Curley notes, 'It's impossible to even retransmit a WebRTC audio packet within a browser; we tried at Discord. The implementation is hard-coded for real-time latency or else.' This creates a fundamental tension between conversational AI requirements and web standards designed for human-to-human communication. LLMs aren't particularly responsive anyway, so the WebRTC optimization may be misaligned with actual AI voice use cases.
author: Luke Curley (cited by Simon Willison)

title: Reinventing Wheels: Andrew Quinn on Learning Through Reimplementation
description: Andrew Quinn shares a profound insight about the guilt of not knowing whether your tool is superseded by 30-year-old implementations. His central thesis: 'This is a trap. You need to reinvent a couple of wheels to get to the edge of what we know about wheel-making, not a thousand wheels, and not zero; probably four or five is sufficient in most domains, maybe closer to twenty or thirty in the most epistemically rigorous and developed fields like mathematics or computer science.' Each wheel you reinvent propels you faster to the true frontier than that same amount of time in idle study, or even five times that amount. This challenges the 'don't reinvent the wheel' conventional wisdom, suggesting that selective reimplementation is actually the most efficient path to true understanding and innovation.
author: Andrew Quinn (cited by Simon Willison)

title: Mitchell Hashimoto: Programming Languages Are Increasingly Not Lock-In
description: Mitchell Hashimoto on Bun migrating from Zig to Rust: 'On the interesting side is how fungible programming languages are nowadays. Programming languages used to be LOCK IN, and they're increasingly not so. You think the Bun rewrite in Rust is good for Rust? Bun has shown they can be in probably any language they want in roughly a week or two. Rust is expendable. Its useful until its not then it can be thrown out.' Simon Willison connects this to a conversation about a company using coding agents to rewrite both iPhone and Android apps to React Native - they chose React Native not because AI couldn't maintain separate apps, but because if it was wrong, they could 'just port back to native' in the future. The cost of language/framework migration has collapsed with AI assistance, fundamentally changing the calculus of technology choices.
author: Mitchell Hashimoto (cited by Simon Willison)

title: datasette-ip-rate-limit 0.1a0: AI-Built Rate Limiting Plugin
description: Simon Willison built a rate limiting plugin for Datasette using 'Codex (GPT-5.5 xhigh)' to block poorly-behaved crawlers hammering the datasette.io site. The plugin provides configurable rate limiting with header-based IP identification, exempt paths (like /static/*), and path-specific rules. Example production configuration: 60 requests per 60-second window for specific demo database paths, with 20-second block duration. Notable that this was built entirely by AI with human supervision - Willison provided requirements, the AI generated the implementation. This showcases how AI coding assistants are shifting developer workflows from implementation to specification and review.
author: Simon Willison

title: datasette 1.0a29: Bug Fix with Dockerfile Reproduction
description: Simon Willison released datasette 1.0a29 with a notable bug fix: a segfault bug due to race condition between Datasette.close() and Database.close(). Willison had added automatic connection closing at the end of each test, but this introduced a race condition where in-flight queries could execute while connection was closing. The solution: 'I ended up solving that by having Codex CLI (with GPT-5.5 xhigh) create a minimal Dockerfile that recreated the bug.' This approach - using AI to create minimal reproduction environments - is an interesting pattern for debugging complex concurrency issues. The release also includes new TokenRestrictions.abbreviated() utility method, improved table display for zero-row tables, and Mobile Safari bug fix.
author: Simon Willison

title: Welcome to the Datasette Blog: Built with OpenAI Codex Desktop
description: Simon Willison launched an official blog for Datasette project, built using 'OpenAI Codex desktop.' Notable feature: the tool has a 'Markdown session transcript export feature' that Willison has 'always wanted.' He shared the actual session transcript that built the blog. This transparency into AI-assisted development is valuable - showing not just the final code but the conversation that produced it. The blog will host Datasette announcements, moving away from scattering updates across different platforms. This represents a pattern: AI tools are enabling smaller teams to build and maintain more infrastructure (like project blogs) that previously wouldn't justify the effort.
author: Simon Willison

title: llm-gemini 0.31: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite No Longer Preview
description: Simon Willison released llm-gemini 0.31 with the update that 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite is no longer a preview.' Willison had previously written about the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Preview model back in March, noting its capabilities and performance characteristics. This graduation from preview to stable status represents Google's continued iteration in the competitive LLM space. The LLM tool ecosystem continues to expand support for multiple model providers, giving developers flexibility to choose models based on cost, performance, and specific capabilities.
author: Simon Willison

title: Government Digital Service: Keep Open Source Open by Default
description: Terence Eden continues coverage of NHS's poorly considered decision to close down open source repositories after Project Glasswing vulnerability reports. Now UK Government Digital Service has joined with 'AI, open code and vulnerability risk in the public sector' published May 14th. Key recommendation: 'Keep open by default. Making everything private adds additional delivery and policy costs, and can reduce reuse and scrutiny. Openness should remain the default posture, with closure used sparingly and deliberately.' Eden interprets this as a 'major escalation' within UK Civil Service, noting it's rare for internal disagreements to spill over publicly. The phrase 'invited to a meeting without biscuits' implies a frosty, no-nonsense discussion. This represents an important institutional stance supporting open source in the public sector, specifically in the context of AI and security research.
author: Simon Willison (citing Terence Eden / GDS)
